clue.text: First Land Commission Report ?

parts.note: read as the earliest official survey of land holdings ordered by a ruler, the great survey William the Conqueror commissioned in 1086

explanation.surface: A heading for the opening paper of some government inquiry into land use.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like the title of a modern report, but the first great survey of English land and its owners was the 1086 record compiled for William I.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1086 survey recorded who held each English estate and what it was worth, so it was the first national land report.

clue.text: Like the sea, polluted by Macbeth's murderous hand ?

definitions.text: Like the sea, polluted by Macbeth's murderous hand ?

parts.words: Like the sea, polluted by Macbeth's murderous hand
parts.note: Macbeth says his bloody hand would 'the multitudinous seas incarnadine, making the green one red': the clue asks what colour the ocean would then be, with a nod to the sea's depth

explanation.surface: A line of literary criticism about the bloodied ocean in Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth II.ii, Macbeth fears that washing his hand would turn all the oceans crimson; 'Like the sea' also points to the first word, since the sea is profound.
explanation.definitionFit: Blood washed into the green ocean would leave it a dark crimson colour, which is the shade named.

clue.text: Bird — one sees her wandering in a 3

parts.note: a cross-reference to the heath entry, Egdon, which is a moor; the page prints 3 where the numbering makes it 13
a hen is a female bird, a 'her' among birds

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's note about a female bird seen roaming somewhere wild.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'a 3', but the heath clue is 13, EGDON, Hardy's moorland. 'wandering in' only places the female bird on that moor.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a common waterbird with a red bill, a member of the rail family found across Britain.

clue.text: Revolutionary body suffers a little sea-change

indicators.note: the 'change' in sea-change tells us the letters of the words before it are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A shift in the coast is described as a sea-change undergone by a rebellious group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary body' looks like a rebel group but means something that orbits. 'change' turns LITTLESEA into the answer; the leading 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A moon or spacecraft revolves around a planet, so it is a body in orbit.

clue.text: We hear you are after a doctor, love!

indicators.note: the sounded piece is placed after A and MO

parts.note: MO is a Medical Officer, an army doctor

indicators.note: these words tell us the next phrase is to be taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: said quickly, the two words sound like the letters U and R

explanation.surface: Someone declares their love for a person who is chasing a physician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' turns 'you are' into the sound of U R, which 'after' puts behind A plus MO, the Medical Officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for love is used in English for a love affair, especially a secret one.

clue.text: Tweedledum or Tweedledee, by agreement

parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's nursery rhyme the twins 'agreed to have a battle', so each is one who fights by agreement

explanation.surface: A quiz question about the twins in Through the Looking-Glass and whether they agree.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme runs 'Tweedledum and Tweedledee agreed to have a battle'; 'by agreement' seems to mean 'either will do', but it is their agreement to fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Each twin agreed to fight the other, so each is a fighter by agreement.

clue.text: The Turk sorts no mails

indicators.note: to sort mail is to put it in a different order, so the words after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Turkish postal clerk is sorting letters but finds none to sort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorts' reshuffles NOMAILS; it looks like a postal verb with 'no mails' as its object.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ottoman subject, named after the dynasty founder Osman, was called this, so it means a Turk.

clue.text: A form of music as opposed to a merryman

parts.note: counter means contrary to or against
Jack Point is the jester (merryman) in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Yeomen of the Guard

explanation.surface: A music lesson contrasting a serious style with the work of a clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'merryman' is a jester; Gilbert and Sullivan's best-known jester is Jack Point in The Yeomen of the Guard.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the technique of combining independent melodic lines, as in a Bach fugue.

clue.text: Expand the ring put round one perhaps

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

indicators.note: taking letters round means turning them about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A jeweller enlarges a ring by fitting it around something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' rearranges PUTONE into PENOUT, after the O from 'the ring'; 'perhaps' only softens the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to unfold or spread wider, like a map being unfolded.

clue.text: It's best to work it backwards, mater

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: the word it is to be read from its end to its start

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, which is Mum

explanation.surface: A child is told the best way to do a task is in reverse, Mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mater' is Latin for mother, as in alma mater; 'backwards' turns only the little word it, and the comma is just punctuation.
explanation.definitionFit: The optimum is the most favourable condition, the best that can be had.

clue.text: Guard is eccentric in a pitched battle

definitions.text: Guard is eccentric in a pitched battle

parts.words: Guard is eccentric in a pitched battle
parts.note: a batsman's guard is the position marked at the crease; this one is off-centre, a cricket match being a battle on a pitch

explanation.surface: A soldier on sentry duty behaves oddly in the middle of a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman 'takes guard' by asking the umpire to line his bat up with a stump; this guard lies between two stumps rather than at the centre, hence 'eccentric'.
explanation.definitionFit: Batsmen choose a guard such as leg stump or centre; this one is halfway between the central stump and the leg stump.

clue.text: Sea-unicorn

parts.note: an Arctic whale whose male has one long spiral tusk, like the horn of the mythical beast

explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic whale's single tusk makes it look like a unicorn of the ocean, and that is its old name.

clue.text: Shipping company is in debt, though tailor-renovated

indicators.note: the company's name sits inside the word for debt

parts.note: being in the red means being in debt
a line is a company running ships on regular routes

explanation.surface: A shipping firm owes money even after a tailor has smartened up its uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shipping company' is the definition-looking start, but the def is the hyphenated 'tailor-renovated' at the end; 'is in' signals the container, and 'though' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A coat that a tailor has renovated has been fitted with a new lining.

clue.text: Native heath — a hardy perennial ?

parts.note: Thomas Hardy's heath in The Return of the Native, which appears again and again in his Wessex books, so a perennial of Hardy's

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on a tough native heather that comes back every year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hardy perennial' looks like gardening but means a recurring feature of Thomas Hardy's novels; 'Native' points to The Return of the Native.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy set The Return of the Native on this fictional Dorset heath and returned to it in other stories.

clue.text: Communicate one to Alphonse without prejudice

parts.note: to impart is to tell or pass on
I is the Roman numeral one
Al is a short form of Alphonse

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to pass a message to a Frenchman without bias.
explanation.walkthrough: IMPART, I (one) and AL, a short form of Alphonse, run in order; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone without prejudice is fair, treating all sides alike.

clue.text: But these openings are mainly not confined to the left

definitions.text: But these openings are mainly not confined to the left

parts.words: But these openings are mainly not confined to the left
parts.note: 'mainly' means on the main, at sea; ships' windows are on both sides, not only on the port (left) side

explanation.surface: A remark that chess openings are not mostly left-wing ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' is the left side of a ship, so windows on ships seem by name to be on the left, yet are found on both sides.
explanation.definitionFit: These round ship's windows take their name from port, though they are set on both sides of a vessel.

clue.text: Sea adventurer — or hired eavesdropper, would you say ?

indicators.note: these words ask us to go by how the phrase is spoken

parts.note: a private ear is a listener for hire, a play on 'private eye'

explanation.surface: A question about whether a pirate could double as a paid snoop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'would you say' makes 'private ear', a hired listener on the model of a private eye, sound like the armed ship's captain licensed to raid enemy shipping.
explanation.definitionFit: A privately owned ship or captain licensed to attack enemy merchant ships was a seagoing adventurer.

clue.text: " In Xanadu … Where blossomed many an bearing tree "

definitions.text: " In Xanadu … Where blossomed many an bearing tree "

parts.words: In Xanadu … Where blossomed many an bearing tree
parts.note: lines from Coleridge's Kubla Khan with a word left out of 'many an ___-bearing tree'

explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's Kubla Khan has 'Where blossomed many an incense-bearing tree'; the clue leaves out the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Coleridge's line describes trees that yield fragrant resin burned for its smell, so the missing word is that resin.

clue.text: After the South Wind, the East appears harsh

indicators.note: the east comes after the wind in the answer

parts.note: Auster is the Roman name for the south wind
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A weather report saying conditions turn harsh when an easterly follows a southerly.
explanation.walkthrough: AUSTER is the Latin south wind; 'After' places E behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere means severe, stern and without comfort.

clue.text: " There's a——girl a-settin', and I know she thinks o' me " (Kipling)

definitions.text: " There's a——girl a-settin', and I know she thinks o' me " (Kipling)

parts.words: There's a——girl a-settin', and I know she thinks o' me
parts.note: a line from Kipling's Mandalay with the name of the country left blank

explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem Mandalay runs 'By the old Moulmein Pagoda, lookin' lazy at the sea, There's a ___ girl a-settin''; the gap is the old name of Myanmar.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's girl waits in the Asian country now called Myanmar, where Moulmein and Mandalay stand.

clue.text: The flower suggests a Latinized dismissal

parts.note: the word for 'go away!' given a Latin-looking ending -ia, as many plant names are

explanation.surface: A botanist notes that a flower's name seems to tell you to go away in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Begone!' is an old dismissal; give it the -ia ending of Latin plant names and you have the flower, really named after Michel Bégon.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a garden plant with showy flowers and lopsided leaves.

clue.text: Took part in the replay, in response to stimulus ?

definitions.meaning: behaved in reply to something that prompted it

explanation.surface: An actor appeared in a repeat performance only because something prompted him.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the word after RE and it means acted again, as in a replay; whole, it is what a nerve does to a stimulus.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting a part again is to re-act; a response to a stimulus is likewise a reply in action.

clue.text: Is gold first incorporated in this tooth?

indicators.note: the abbreviation comes first, before the other two pieces

parts.note: taken as written
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A dentist asks whether gold was the first material put into this tooth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' puts INC (incorporated) ahead of IS and OR, heraldry's gold; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The sharp front teeth used for cutting food are this kind.

clue.text: Receive what's stolen from trees

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the word that follows, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes in fruit that has been taken from trees.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots law to reset is to receive stolen goods; 'from' makes the answer out of TREES.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots usage resetting is handling stolen property, the fence's crime.

clue.text: Gaunt Rider

definitions.meaning: Rider ..., author of King Solomon's Mines

explanation.definitionFit: A gaunt face looks worn out; Henry Rider Haggard wrote adventure novels.

clue.text: Workers stripped for inaction on the beach ?

definitions.text: Workers stripped for inaction on the beach ?

parts.words: Workers stripped for inaction on the beach
parts.note: people who lie idle in the sun with clothes off, and also workers who treat stripped hides to make leather

explanation.surface: Labourers are undressed and punished for idling at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers' are leather-dressers who work on stripped hides, but the clue also means sunbathers who lie stripped and idle on the sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunbathers browning their skin are so called, as are workers who cure hides into leather.

clue.text: Gareth's bride, by later report

parts.note: The old teller says Gareth wed Lyonors, 'But he, that told it later' names her sister

explanation.surface: A news item about who a man called Gareth actually married.
explanation.walkthrough: Malory has Gareth marry Lyonors; Tennyson closes his Idyll of the King by saying a 'later' teller gives the bride as the damsel who guided him.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tennyson's version, Gareth weds the sharp-tongued damsel who led him on his quest.

clue.text: Where one man takes eight records ?

definitions.text: Where one man takes eight records ?

parts.words: Where one man takes eight records
parts.note: the BBC radio show in which a guest chooses eight discs to take into imagined isolation

explanation.surface: A question about a solo traveller packing music for a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Desert Island Discs, a long-running BBC radio show, has each guest pick eight records to take to a place where they would be alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The radio show imagines a castaway on a remote uninhabited spot with only eight records.
